articles.title: Meta Infrastructure Spend Reaches Negative Cash Flow Inflection Point
articles.content: LivestreamMenuMeta stock sank almost 7% Thursday as free cash flow turned negative and the company raised the floor of its expected capex spend.Prices for the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs.Meta also revealed it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock.In this article Meta shares slumped nearly 7% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures. The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans. Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion. Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter. The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth." Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing. Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted. Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable with the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for. — CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

articles.title: Hong Kong Allocates Hundred Million Dollars to Automated Procurement
articles.content: Hong Kong’s urban redevelopment body will spend no more than HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will verify tender applications using automated AI systems, in response to accusations of corruption in the wake of the deadly Tai Po fire. Wang Fuk Court on May 4, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The sum amounts to a third of the full HK$300 million that the government is allocating to the Urban Renewal Authority (URA) as announced in the government’s 2026-27 Budget. The funds are aimed at reforming the body’s Smart Tender scheme. The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to provide property owners with an electronic tendering platform to recruit contractors. By anonymising the tender procedure, the system is supposed to prevent interference and bolster competition, but it cannot control who participates in or withdraws from a tender exercise. “[U]p to HK$100 million will be used as start-up funding to establish a dedicated subsidiary, recruit a professional team and develop an ‘AI-first’ automated workflow system for in-depth data verification and precise analysis,” URA Managing Director Donald Choi said in the body’s 2025-26 annual report , issued last week. The remaining funds will be used to subsidise owners using the upgraded support service, the authority said. The deadly apartment fire at Wang Fuk Court in November last year killed 168 people and displaced thousands of residents. The estate was undergoing a large-scale renovation project costing some HK$330 million when the fire broke out. A public inquiry held this year exposed the contractor’s use of substandard materials, allegedly collusive bidding practices, and rubber-stamp inspections , as well as a toothless regulatory regime that effectively operated on an honour system. Urban Renewal Authority. Photo: GovHK. During one of the hearings, the authority’s lawyer said that the Smart Tender platform, which anonymises the bidding process, was merely “ a shield, but not a fortress ” against illegal tender practice. The URA’s Choi said in the report that the fire “drew public attention to systemic issues in the building rehabilitation sector and heightened calls for the enhancement of support services for building owners.” To reform the tender appraisal system, the authority will set up stringent whitelists for works consultants and contractors, and conduct tendering procedures on behalf of owners. “However, it is important to emphasise that the maintenance malpractices exposed by the fire stem from long-standing systemic shortcomings and entrenched vested interests within the building maintenance sector,” Choi said. “Preventing similar tragedies requires concerted efforts by the Government, regulatory authorities, industry participants, relevant stakeholders and building owners to address these issues at both institutional and operational levels.” Safeguard press freedom; keep HKFP free for all readers by supporting our team Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Share on Mail (Opens in new window) Mail Share on Print (Opens in new window) Print Support HKFP   |   Policies & Ethics   |   Error/typo?   |   Contact   |   Newsletter   |  Transparency & Annual Report  |  Apps Monthly HK$150 HK$250 HK$500 Other Donation amount per month HK$ per month Recurring donors unlock 8 benefits : Members get a free HKFP deer keyring or tote; ad-free browsing and no pop-ups; full access to HKFP Monitor , exclusive Tim Hamlett opinion columns; HKFP feature previews; 15% off all merch ; Editor’s Blogs ; and early access to our Annual/Transparency Report . articles.title: Brazilian Prosecutors Force Meta to Cease Arbitrary Election Censorship
articles.content: 21 de outubro de 2026 21:03 Por Marcelo Oliveira Faça da Pública sua fonte preferida Nos adicione como fonte preferencial no Google. Não deixe a Publica sumir Nos adicione como fonte preferencial no Google. --> Justiça eleições 2026 Meta Ministério Público política redes sociais Em dois movimentos distintos, um judicial e outro extrajudicial, o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) quer barrar bloqueios, suspensões de contas e restrições de alcance promovidos pela Meta no Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp e Threads. Na Justiça Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, o MPF ajuizou nesta quarta-feira, 21 de outubro, uma ação civil pública, com pedido de urgência. Em outra frente, a Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão (PFDC) enviou recomendação à Meta, cobrando providências imediatas. A ação lida especificamente com as denúncias que fazem parte da representação feita pelas organizações Ctrl+Z, Artigo 19, Conectas e Sleeping Giants Brasil, que mostram que a Meta bloqueou conteúdos políticos pró-Lula e contra Flávio. A Agência Pública mostrou que além dos bloqueios, a plataforma derrubou perfis com acusação de terrorismo e nudez, mesmo não havendo conteúdos nesse sentido. A Procuradoria pede o restabelecimento imediato de contas, páginas e conteúdos afetados pelas restrições apontadas na representação. A ação pede ainda que a Justiça Federal proíba o uso exclusivo de algoritmos para decisões de bloqueio de conteúdo e que as futuras reavaliações e análises de recursos sejam conduzidas obrigatoriamente por equipes humanas especializadas , com a fixação de multa diária de R$ 500 mil por conta afetada, em caso de descumprimento. O MPF apurou que as restrições arbitrárias impostas pela companhia foram operadas por meio de algoritmos automatizados, sem notificação clara sobre as supostas violações ou oportunidade de contestação por canal efetivo com revisão humana. Essa prática provocou o enfraquecimento do engajamento de conteúdos cívicos e o cerceamento do debate democrático. Ao público, no dia 16, a Meta reconheceu que “a conta de anúncios da campanha de Lula foi desativada por engano por pouco mais de 1 hora”, mas afirmou que não se tratou de “razões políticas”. Uma das vítimas das restrições foi a arquiteta Carolina Martins, 43, de Brasília. Ela criou um grupo e uma comunidade visando angariar apoio para a candidatura de Lula no segundo turno. O grupo chegou a ser derrubado, acusado de “terrorismo” sem fundamentação pela empresa. Ela teve a conta de WhatsApp derrubada e ainda está sofrendo outras restrições da Meta. Ao divulgar esta semana a proposta do presidente Lula para que ambos os candidatos abram seu sigilo bancário, feita após o debate da rede Bandeirantes, Martins postou uma imagem que dizia “Flavio Abra o Sigilo”. Na segunda-feira, dia 19, ela foi suspensa pela Meta de postar links em suas publicações no Instagram até 16 de novembro sob a acusação de “práticas comerciais proibidas”. Já a recomendação, que é uma medida extrajudicial para uma empresa ou ente público realizar medidas para corrigir uma ilegalidade, foi expedida pela Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão, em Brasília, e direcionada diretamente à Meta para que a companhia adote medidas urgentes de transparência e proteção à liberdade de expressão nas redes Facebook, Instagram, Threads e WhatsApp durante o período eleitoral. À empresa foi dado prazo de 48 horas para responder se acatará as recomendações do MPF e para detalhar as providências que serão adotadas durante o segundo turno das eleições, além de 30 dias para apresentar um relatório conclusivo. A medida da PFDC vem depois da instauração de investigação no último dia 13 na qual o MPF pediu à Meta uma série de informações. A companhia enviou uma resposta ao MPF no dia 19 de outubro, complementada ontem, 20.  Nas respostas, segundo a PFDC, a Meta teria alegado, em síntese, que a sua moderação se basearia nos Padrões da Comunidade e na legislação local, que não levaria em conta a orientação política ou ideológica dos usuários. As respostas foram consideradas genéricas pelo MPF e não abordaram as moderações indevidas e não esclareceram caso a caso no que se baseou cada restrição, conforme demandado no ofício da semana passada. A manifestação da Meta não mencionou as suspensões fundadas em enquadramentos graves (como terrorismo e abuso sexual), nem das remoções que teriam ocorrido após denúncias em massa. A recomendação à Meta é assinada pelo Procurador Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão, Paulo Thadeu Gomes da Silva, e mais cinco procuradores do MPF que atuam na área de direitos humanos. articles.title: Canadian Surveillance Expansion Bill Meets Broad Privacy Rights Pushback
articles.content: Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) Take action Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22 As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight. Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. Take action Canadians: defend your privacy and security

articles.title: Australian Industry Deploys Autonomous Agents Ahead of Federal Regulation
articles.content: Advertisement Australian businesses are moving beyond the first wave of workplace artificial intelligence, as employees adopt AI agents and companies begin to work out what happens when the technology takes on tasks rather than simply helping people complete them. HP’s 2026 Work Relationship Index found 56 per cent of Australian knowledge workers – employees whose jobs primarily involve working with information rather than manual tasks – now use work-provided AI daily or weekly, up from 38 per cent a year earlier. Some 45 per cent use AI agents, putting Australia ahead of the developed-market average. Australian businesses are moving beyond AI experimentation as workers adopt AI agents and companies rethink workflows, security and oversight. iStock The figures challenge the idea that Australian workers have been reluctant to embrace AI. But they also point to a harder phase of adoption, where businesses must decide which tasks can be delegated to AI, who remains accountable for the result and how autonomous systems should interact with people and existing workflows. Brad Pulford, HP vice president and managing director for Australia and New Zealand, says the change is already visible in the way employees use the technology. Advertisement “There’s a degree of scepticism in the public conversation about AI at the moment, but look at how people are actually using it,” says Pulford. “The job isn’t done. For many businesses, awareness isn’t the issue, it’s working out how to give their teams context and a clear road map, making sure people know why AI is being introduced, what it means for their role, and how it helps them do their best work.” KPMG Australia has also found businesses pushing further into AI. Its July 2026 AI Pulse found 89 per cent of Australian organisations expected AI to remain a top investment priority, while 83 per cent reported active chief executive ownership of AI initiatives. The report found agentic AI was shifting the focus from experimentation towards execution. Pulford says the consequences extend beyond individual productivity to the way work itself is organised. “When someone uses AI to draft a document, that’s their own workflow. When agents handle multi-step tasks, it changes how work moves between teams, who signs off on what, and what a role is for.” Advertisement From pilots to workflows HP’s research also found adoption is uneven within organisations, with Australian knowledge workers trailing IT decision-makers by 19 percentage points and business leaders by 16 percentage points in their use of agentic AI. Pulford says companies need to treat the arrival of agents as workflow redesign rather than another software rollout. “Leaders should be clear where accountability sits, be deliberate about what runs where, and involve employees in shaping the new way of working,” Pulford says. Human oversight becomes more important as AI takes on more complex work. HP’s global research found 78 per cent of proficient AI users were confident they understood where AI ended and their own judgment began, compared with 52 per cent of basic users. Advertisement “Human judgment is the part that gets least attention. Leaders should be clear about what data can go where, define the decisions that always need a human, and give people the training to interrogate an AI output rather than accept it,” Pulford says. Deciding where AI runs The spread of workplace AI is also forcing businesses to decide which workloads should run locally and which belong in the cloud. Generative AI services have largely relied on cloud-based models, but newer business devices can perform some AI processing locally, an approach often described as “AI at the edge”. Processing AI at the edge can bring computing closer to the employee and the task. Companies can choose between on-device and cloud processing according to the task, the data involved and the computing power required. Advertisement Pulford says security and cost are significant factors in that decision. More than half of enterprise leaders surveyed for HP’s Work Relationship Index cited security as a major barrier to AI investment, while cost was another concern across businesses of different sizes. “Start with the data and the task, not the technology,” Pulford says. “Workloads involving sensitive information, or needing speed and offline reliability, often suit on-device processing. Large-scale models and collaborative workflows may belong in the cloud. Most organisations will need both.” Running suitable workloads locally can also avoid sending every request to a cloud service and the associated per-query costs. Pulford says businesses should assess workloads according to sensitivity, performance and cost rather than assume every AI task belongs in the same computing environment. Those decisions are also changing what businesses require from workplace computers. HP’s Work Relationship Index found 51 per cent of Australian knowledge workers nominated faster, more reliable devices as something that would help them do their best work. Yet only about one-third said they had been given an upgraded computer to run AI, compared with about half of business leaders and IT decision-makers. Advertisement “The expectation of the workplace PC is fundamentally changing. It is no longer simply a device for accessing applications,” Pulford says. “Increasingly, it is becoming an intelligent platform where AI, security and collaboration come together.” HP’s Intel Powered EliteBook X G2i is one example, combining dedicated on-device AI processing with enterprise security and AI-enabled collaboration tools. Businesses can determine which workloads operate on the device and which remain in the cloud according to responsiveness, connectivity and security requirements. The human boundary Deciding where AI runs is only part of the equation. As agents take on sequences of tasks across business systems, companies also have to decide where their authority ends. Advertisement An employee using generative AI to help write an email can check the output before sending it. An agent carrying out several tasks across different systems raises more complicated questions about permissions, data access, mistakes and responsibility. Pulford says guardrails need to be established before agents begin moving information through company systems rather than added later. “Security, governance and human judgment aren’t brakes on AI, they’re what lets you scale it with confidence,” he says. “Guardrails and good judgment are what turn adoption into something you can trust.” The next phase of workplace AI will be less about whether Australian businesses use the technology than what they allow it to do. As agents move from assisting individual employees to carrying out work across teams and systems, businesses will have to make explicit choices about where machines act, where people decide and who remains responsible when the two work together. As AI reshapes how Australians work, having the right technology underpin that shift matters more than ever. articles.content: No actual digits or cats were harmed beyond the number crunching that went into this LLM poisoning experiment Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published thu 22 Oct 2026 // 20:57 UTC Make us preferred on Google PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk 1 day ago Jensen Huang sends in the robot ducks to sell Nvidia's AI-everywhere vision 1 day ago It's a bird, it's a plane...well, more of a spinning parachute, but really it's a droppable robot boat 14 days ago OpenAI GPT-6 Astra really good at supply chain attacks, UK gov warns 24 days ago Australian cops cuff alleged TeamPCP masterminds August 28, 2026 Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense. A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning. The technique, dubbed MuTRAP , is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.  MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills. The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006 . "Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service.  "It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources." The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word. The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B. Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper. No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine. But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's proposed defense known as PROTEA , which employs an LLM to judge and evaluate the security of task plans (and should not be confused with several other research projects named PROTEA ). There are already ample real-world examples of robots that have violated the first of science fiction writer Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics – "A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm." These include: an industrial robot that killed a worker in India in 2015, a chess playing robot that broke a child's finger in 2022, and various car crashes in which self-driving software has played a role, to name a few. articles.title: American Innovation Clusters Reorganize Under Severe DOGE Budget Reductions
articles.content: A year and a half after the so-called Department of Government Efficiency terminated the contracts of 17 Regional Innovation Clusters , the Small Business Administration announced nine new awardees for the initiative to spur technological development across the country. The new RICs, unveiled earlier this month , include defense-focused clusters in Arizona, southern California, Louisiana, northern Michigan and central/south Florida; biotech organizations in Tampa Bay and the Mid-Atlantic region; an advanced manufacturing group in San Antonio and Austin; and a transportation cohort in the Ozarks. The agency’s initial callout for applications in August 2025 — just a few months after DOGE delivered its cuts — sought organizations focused on advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, nuclear microreactors, quantum tech and emerging systems, AI, cybersecurity, IT, and semiconductors.  An SBA spokesperson said in an email to FedScoop that the agency’s prioritization of defense and manufacturing didn’t reflect a pivot away from AI, cyber and other tech areas, but instead folded into the administration’s focus on “rebuilding American industrial dominance.” “The new awards identify the industries the clusters will serve, rather than every technology they will support,” the spokesperson said, “so the emphasis on defense and manufacturing does not represent a shift away from those technologies.” Launched in 2010, the RIC initiative was conceived as a relatively low-cost way to fuel innovation in geographic regions across the country, serving as connective tissue for businesses, suppliers and institutions.  At $7 million via congressionally appropriated funding through SBA’s entrepreneurial development programs, the topline figure backing the nine new RICs — which join three that survived DOGE — is less than the $9 million allocated to the program in fiscal 2025 and 2026.  But the White House’s initial fiscal 2027 budget zeroed out the RIC initiative altogether. And the SBA spokesperson said the agency has “introduced new pathways to capital for businesses in critical industries and tailored resources to help them expand production.” Jason Rittenberg, who worked with the SBA and several RICs while serving as vice president of the Ohio-based science and tech nonprofit SSTI , said it was “a bit of a surprise” to see the new awards go out given Trump administration moves to delay funding and cut contracts at the National Institutes of Health , the National Science Foundation and other agencies .  But the RIC program “has shown meaningful benefits for businesses and employees,” Rittenberg noted. And DOGE — while now more institutionalized across the government — is a bit more in the rearview, giving applicants the impression that to a “certain degree, things have settled down a little bit,” he added. “The administration doesn’t seem to be spending all the money that they’re appropriated [but] they’re also following through more often on the announcements that they are actually putting out the door,” said Rittenberg, now the principal of Excel Regional Solutions . “So maybe groups are also just starting to read it as a little bit less risky than maybe things would have felt … a year ago.” The SBA spokesperson said the discontinued RICs “failed to deliver results for small businesses” and the program is now refocused “on reindustrialization across critical industries.”  Heath Naquin, who leads the Mid-Atlantic Biomanufacturing Scale-Up Cluster and previously served as a special adviser to SBA’s Office of Investment and Innovation , downplayed any concerns about the program’s recent past ahead of the application process.  The new RIC, which will enlist biomanufacturing organizations in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, and Washington, D.C., should help highlight “all the assets that are across the entire region” and “leverage additional resources” for the groups, he said. “There’s money going in biomanufacturing all over and onshoring, great, but let’s not recreate the wheel here,” said Naquin, whose day job is senior vice president for innovation and new ventures at University City Science Center in Philadelphia. “Here’s a legitimate hub … and we really do hope it helps build up the reputation and the business friendliness.” The new RIC contracts were enacted Sept. 30 and will each run for two years. The SBA spokesperson said the new RICs represent organizations with “proven experience supporting critical industries and technologies” that will “help small businesses in those industries commercialize innovations, expand domestic production, and strengthen supply chains essential to America’s industrial base.” Rittenberg was skeptical of the program’s future in the aftermath of DOGE’s targeting of it, but he’s been encouraged by the SBA’s recent RIC moves, including putting out a request for information that asked the small business tech community to weigh in on what they’d like to see going forward.  “You see the questions that the agency is asking, you can kind of get a sense of where their mind is,” he said. “I think doing that and then following up with the competition probably helped people understand that this was something that was being given serious thought in the agency, and maybe did help people feel more comfortable putting together … a serious and competitive proposal.”

articles.title: Smart Home Hardware Silently Consumes Massive Household Network Bandwidth
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess 3 terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google . The Google Gemini–powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network. While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the past 10 days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September. Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices and that it has rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.” Courtesy of Google Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the past week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the past week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day. If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for which device could be at fault. How to Check Your Device Usage Courtesy of Amazon You have a couple of options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses. comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router , and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how: Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in. Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour). You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab. You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone. Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how: Open the Deco or Tether app. Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage . What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information. Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter , you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface. (It usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app.) If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations. But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the past seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or over the past three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home. But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector. Why Should You Check? It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the 2 terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a 3-terabyte bug slowing your whole network. Power up with unlimited access to WIRED . articles.title: Hyperscale Data Center Construction Fuels Industrial Resource and Grid Clashes
articles.content: With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers , America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses. The new raft of promises from the world’s richest companies comes as anti-data center sentiment has become a potent issue in the midterm elections , with control of Congress and 36 governors’ offices on the line. Despite backing from President Donald Trump , the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic . Community opposition that blocks municipal permits has become a bottleneck, and tech giants could face even more challenges if voters next month elect more public officials who are skeptical of data centers. The tech industry says it has gotten the message. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build. Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics. Devi Thomas, Google’s global head of community development and engagement, told AP that she wouldn’t call resistance to data centers a “backlash,” but that “there are often community questions to be addressed.” “Early public consultation is increasingly a very important part of the process. We have done as much as we can to make sure communities are involved early on,” Thomas said. Earlier this month, Amazon rolled out its “Amazon Data Center Commitment,” including pledges to improve the environmental rating of its backup diesel generators and disclose more about its data centers’ energy and water use . It also said — as have Microsoft and Google — that it had stopped requiring government officials to sign non-disclosure agreements. The use of non-disclosure agreements has meant people in host communities may know little or nothing about a project until it shows up on a municipal board’s voting agenda. Besides that, tech companies often have hidden their involvement in a project behind a code name and developers who do the legwork with local governments, critics and other developers say. That practice “raises people’s suspicion as to what’s truly happening,” said Anita Verma-Lallian, a developer with data center projects in Arizona. Meta is always evaluating how well it shares information with communities, said Lindsay Elin, Meta’s vice president of public policy and external affairs. “As part of that work, we are reviewing our use of non-disclosure agreements,” she said in a statement to the AP. In a report this month that sharply criticized data center giants including Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, several Senate Democrats said companies have used non-disclosure agreements to freeze out the public. The report also said the companies aggressively seek state and local tax breaks and do not cover the entire cost of the electric-grid buildout needed for energy-hungry data centers. The dominant players in the industry — Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft — project they’ll spend more than $600 billion this year combined on capital projects, primarily data center construction in the U.S. Even as the companies prepare to spend more to entice communities — payments that some critics call “bribes” — Trump urged them in a social media post Wednesday to pay people and communities a “dividend” if they “want to make their Data Centers popular.” “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.,” Trump wrote. Meta and Amazon said recently they will each spend $1 billion on financial incentives to host communities in the coming years, on top of millions they already spend to support schools, charities and job training. Google says its investments in local programs in data center communities will reach $1 billion by the end of 2027. Microsoft has pointed to a couple local tax breaks that it will forego. And Google recently said for all of its new data center campuses, the company will pay full real property taxes on the buildings and land. The companies have known since last fall that community opposition was becoming a serious problem. Data center demand began driving up electric bills last year across a 13-state electricity grid stretching from Illinois to New Jersey and Maryland, angering ratepayers. The outcry led to promises from the tech giants to pay the cost of the power infrastructure to feed their data centers, while Microsoft rolled out its five-point “Community-First AI Infrastructure” plan. Data centers’ critics aren’t persuaded. Sam Burleigh, who helped start Concerned Citizens of Montour County in rural northern Pennsylvania to fight a potential Amazon-backed data center project, said the company’s commitments are “propaganda.” “What I see is them realizing they have more resistance than they ever dreamt of. And so now they have to find some way, some method to break through that resistance,” Burleigh said. Kathryn Hoffman, executive director of the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy, which has sued over two prospective Google data centers, said she sees Google doing more public relations outreach, but she doesn’t see it doing more to disclose critical details about its plans. In an Aug. 18 memo, the Senate Republicans’ national campaign arm crystallized the midterm election pressure on the tech giants. It warned the tech sector that it must “fix the toxic brand of an entire segment of the economy” or risk long-term fallout in elections. That included addressing “who benefits, who pays, and why a community should want one.” Drew Nations, a developer in North Carolina, said developers need to aggressively address quality-of-life complaints from neighbors. That includes shielding neighbors from noise and data centers from public view so they aren’t an eyesore, and they need to forego “corporate welfare” such as the lucrative sales tax exemptions that nearly 40 states offer. Those tax breaks leave regular people thinking, “‘So you’re saying that this multi-multi-billion if not trillion-dollar company gets tax breaks and I don’t?'” Nations said. Meta, Google, Microsoft and Amazon collectively reported more than $300 billion in net income in their most recent fiscal year. Spending to promote data centers has been on the rise. The Data Center Coalition, a trade association whose members include the tech giants, said it has spent more than $10 million running pro-data center ads in 10 states on TV and elsewhere. Data center giant QTS and a group that doesn’t disclose its donors, Build American AI, also began ad campaigns this year. Meanwhile, angry residents continue to flood once-sleepy municipal board meetings, pressuring officials to reject data center proposals. More municipalities are passing data center moratoriums and Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it saw sustained local opposition to dozens of projects in the April-to-June quarter, its latest reporting period. Balaji Tammabattula, chief operating officer of BaRupOn, which develops data center campuses, said the pressure of the midterms has helped developers understand how crucial community support is to a project’s success. “It’s impossible to build without them,” he said. articles.title: Autonomous Android Emulation Enables Full Apple iOS Firmware Execution
articles.content: HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel ( xnu-8796.121.2 , the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible. It runs in two places: POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot , the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android; QEMU ( virt , aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed. This repository is half of the project: Repository What hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl , prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc. Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing ( gpu=1 ). More in Screenshots . Works Does not work (yet) Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges) Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland) Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits) Up to 8 CPU cores ( cpus=8 ), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno ( gpu=1 , OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation) Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos) Data that iOS writes survives a reboot ( var_store=1 ufs_write=1 ); iOS root volume on the phone's flash Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log. prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW. Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch): sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64 (Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64 ; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.) git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios cd hackios common/setup.sh # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host ios165/fetch.sh # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min) common/build.sh qemu-virt # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there) common/run.sh qemu-virt # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes. Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back: swipe from the left edge. Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑ / ↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers. From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250 , qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71 , qemu/touch.py key home ; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png . Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s. Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd . You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot , and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage. The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android: adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/ # GPU (gpu=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/ # Wi-Fi (wifi=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/ # sound (adsp=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/ # haptics (Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.) common/build.sh redwood GL=1 # images + out/redwood-boot.img common/run.sh redwood 900 # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session or step by step with xl : ./xl enter # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link ./xl ramdisk # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE= " touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1 " ./xl run ./xl screenshot shot.png ./xl reboot # back to Android ./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...). Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot . It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above). common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest. Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk ) and clang lld python perl . Details: xnu/README.md . xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2). Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file). UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it. After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/ . common/new-device.sh < codename > path/to/device.dtb # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree Then follow docs/PORTING.md : the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ ( redwood.conf , qemu-virt.conf , _template.conf ). fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application) │ stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol), │ watchdog, receives the kernel's log ▼ XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform) ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp) ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies) ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU) ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound ▼ iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd │ (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only) └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.driver) The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES ( kern.exec_inject ). Path What common/ setup.sh (workspace), build.sh / run.sh (per device), new-device.sh , devices/*.conf , ugit xl drives the phone over USB: loader, kernel runs, logs, screenshots, screen and sound recording xnuloader/ the loader: loader.c (UEFI application), mkpayload.py (kernel + images + arguments container) xnu/ our XNU changes: patch, new files, apply.sh / export.sh xnu-deps/ everything for building XNU on Linux: setup.sh , tool wrappers, stubs xnu-build.sh , xnu-env.sh kernel build uefi/ , mkxnuimg.py the UEFI port and packing the boot image for fastboot boot wifi/lx/ the layer on which Linux's Wi-Fi driver builds for our kernel qemu/ QEMU runs, touch input, screenshots, stack symbolication tools/ recording ( recording.py , sound.py ), UFS/flash tools, mk-ath11k.sh , new-workspace.sh , host tests prebuilt/ built kernel, loader and UEFI pieces ( NOTICES.md for the third-party code in the kernel) docs/ screenshots, checks.md , PORTING.md Session log: QEMU's stdout or logs/HHMMSS-run.log from the phone. RC_JOBS=rc.jobs.tour REST=1 userland/build.sh — an image that unlocks and opens every app of the first page. userabort: in the log is the stack of a process that called abort() ; usertrap: (with systrace=1 ) — crashes. Live stacks (QEMU): qemu/touch.py stacks NAME , then qemu/symstack.py LOG NAME (needs ipsw ). How a check can lie to you: docs/checks.md . From the phone's screen, one session ( GL=1 REST=1 , gpu=1 ): No iOS files are in the repositories: ios165/fetch.sh downloads them from Apple's CDN to your machine. xnu/ is a derivative work of XNU and is distributed under APSL 2.0, like XNU itself; prebuilt/mach.* is the kernel built from it. It also contains ath11k (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) and FreeBSD LinuxKPI code (BSD-2-Clause): see prebuilt/NOTICES.md . xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libzbitmap/ and xnu-deps/build/lzbitmap/ — libzbitmap (Corellium LLC, MIT here); xnu/files/bsd/miscfs/apfs/libdeflate/ — libdeflate 1.24 (Eric Biggers, MIT, COPYING there). ath11k, Linux and FreeBSD sources are not in the repository: tools/mk-ath11k.sh fetches pinned releases. wifi/lx/patches/*.patch are our changes to FreeBSD headers; the rest of wifi/lx/ is ours. uefi/files/Binaries/redwood and prebuilt/uefi/SILICIUM_UEFI.fd contain UEFI drivers from the phone's Xiaomi firmware, distributed the way Project Silicium distributes them for other devices; prebuilt/uefi/mkbootimg.py — AOSP, Apache-2.0. This repository is licensed under the Apple Public Source License 2.0 : our changes to XNU are a derivative of XNU and must be, and our other code here (loader, scripts) is released under the same license. Third-party code keeps its own license, as listed above. OOSEX GANG — @oodze (founder), @netusd , @wannqn , @hxfuxyyXD . News: t.me/oosexgangdevs .

articles.title: Venture Capital Abandons Slide Decks for Live Autonomous Prototypes
articles.content: Last month (actually it was August—I’ve been busy), my desperate plea to founders to please stop sending AI slop decks went viral. I wrote it because my Monday-morning pitch deck review routine had gone from exciting to neutral to mildly annoying to downright soul-sucking in the course of a year. Decks used to be like a bag of Bertie Botts Every-Flavored Beans—some blah, some gross, some absolutely delightful. Today, it’s all vanilla and completely indistinguishable. I heard from a lot of you in response. Fellow investors adamantly agreed. Most VCs can tell when a deck is AI-generated, and are equally annoyed at the sameness. The deeper issue isn’t about the deck itself—everyone I heard from has the same allergic reaction when it’s clear that AI didn’t just design it—it did the thinking, too. Investors weren’t alone in this—anyone who has to sift through inbound pitches for a living is in the same camp. In particular, journalists and editors in my network report that their inboxes have exploded with PR pitch slop, at an exponentially higher volume than VCs. As a VC and contributor, my inbox and I concur. The one group I didn’t hear much from this time are founders . . . at least not in public. I think the advice hit hard. And I get it. You hate making decks. You think they’re a time-sucking exercise in futility. You spend hundreds of hours perfecting the damn thing only for some VC to have its agent summarize it and, at best, spend 20 seconds reading it. I raise capital for my fund too—so believe you me, I hate my pitch deck too. Maybe it’s time to ditch them altogether. One founder in particular reached out, and their comment made me pause. “What’s the point?” they said. “If VCs are using AI to review them, why shouldn’t I use AI to write them?” Is every VC skipping the deck? Maybe I’m the last one still looking at them (like that time I read 597 résumés last year). I decided to try and find out. A couple of weeks ago, I fielded a quick poll on LinkedIn to find out if most VCs are, in fact, using AI to review pitch decks. Then I spoke, texted, and emailed with a few of the respondents. The results were eye-opening: 72% of VCs use AI to review pitch decks, the vast majority as an augmentation of their process (39% put decks through an AI review before human review, while 29% did human review followed by AI review). It bears noting that 28% don’t use AI at all for this purpose—at least not yet. And only a tiny number use AI alone, with no human review at all. Considering that just a couple of years ago, 99% of VCs were not using AI at all, these numbers should be taken as a snapshot of a moving trend. And that trend is definitely moving toward more AI, not less. When I asked a few VCs to help me understand why, responses came in two camps. The first was about volume. Here’s Rebecca Mitchell, a GP at Scrub Capital : “We get over 50 deals a week, sometimes two dozen a day. I couldn’t possibly look at it all properly.” And B. Pagels-Minor, founder of DVRGNT Ventures : “For me, AI in venture is about scale. I do want to use technology to help us see how much of the world we could potentially diligence without major human interaction.” The second theme was about automation. Take, for example, Ben Orthlieb, GP of Blue Moon VC , a fully AI-operated VC firm. At Blue Moon, AI runs “everything, including LP comms, accounting, company analysis, meeting prep, founder screening.” In this model, Ben doesn’t review any decks at all. “I use [AI] to analyze companies before I meet them and generate meeting outlines with key questions based on the analysis and their backgrounds. My AI associate gives me an in-depth review of the company, its market, and its competition. . . . I don’t need a deck.” Ben’s fully AI-powered operating model is still unusual in venture capital. The question for founders is: Will it stay an outlier or become the norm? To really understand what’s behind the desire for speed and scale in VC, it’s helpful to reflect on the extremely dramatic industry-wide changes that VCs have faced in a very short period of time. First up, the dramatic concentration of capital into megafunds. In Q1 this year, 75% of all LP dollars went to just five funds . This trend is so pronounced that even historically disciplined USV announced its latest fund at close to a billion dollars , more than three times the size of its previous one. The second big trend is the velocity of today’s winners. A select few AI startups are growing blazingly fast, sometimes in traction, sometimes in valuation, sometimes in both. Combine that with some very real examples of superfast, superlarge exits—like Stripe’s $7.5 billion acquisition of OpenRouter just three years after the latter was founded. Or Anthropic, which is just five years old, and is widely expected to IPO this year, with some analysts predicting close to or more than a capital-T Trillion-dollar valuation. Let’s just think about that for a second. A trillion dollars in enterprise value created in just five years. It’s really quite something. Meanwhile, there are more founders than ever too. I don’t have great data on this, but the trend is clear. For instance, 20 years ago, only an estimated 3% to 5% of Harvard Business School graduates started a company before or around graduation. Last year it was 17%. Jeff Bussgang, a VC at Flybridge and senior lecturer at HBS , told me this past spring that about 30% of HBS students are doing “something entrepreneurial” while in school. That was definitely not the case when I was there. To summarize: There are more founders than ever before. The size of the prize is bigger than ever before. The winners win faster than ever before. The biggest funders have more money than ever before. In other words: a perfect storm, the result of which is consensus capital . VCs are furiously competing for “legible” founders, the ones that megafunds (and everyone that aims to coinvest with them) believe are likeliest to deliver a hyperscaling win, ideally before someone else spots them and throws an eye-wateringly huge term sheet their way. VCs now need to find these founders as fast and decisively as humanly possible, which these days really means humanly im possible, AI-possible. The days of relationship-building VC are behind us. Not permanently, I hope. Maybe permanently, I fear. (P.S. Not every VC has become a legibility-focused “trillicorn” [trillion-dollar unicorn] hunter with zero price sensitivity . . . a lot have, but not all.) Because really, a great pitch deck just won’t cut it. In this market, the only founders raising successfully are consensus founders—i.e., the “legible” ones; i.e., the ones that investors believe will win, and therefore can raise so much money so quickly and easily that the expectation of success is a self-fulfilling prophecy, at least when it comes to early fundraising. (Don’t get me started on the huge amount of bias that’s packed into that last run-on sentence. That’s a topic for another day.) And the difference in experience between “legible” and “illegible” founders is not so much a gap anymore; it’s a chasm. As a result, you see founders today desperately trying to figure out a way to become legible to all these trillicorn-hunting VCs—contorting themselves to fit the pattern, having fun with math on their traction, overstating their background, playing power games with prospective early backers. To their detriment, I think. Lying is a straight-up no-no. The hype-y FOMO stuff works well enough to get meetings—it might even work to get a few checks in your round. But it’s manipulative and shallow and, I would argue, not how you build a strong cap table and a strong company. The way I see it, there are only three things that make a founder truly legible—and very helpfully, they all start with T’s. So I hereby coin: Trajectory. This is an obvious one. If you’re Mira Murati breaking out of OpenAI, or Travis Kalanick raising for his next thing, investors know what you can do and are hungry to jump on board. Less famous names fit here too—the PhDs working on boundary-pushing science and robotics, talented technical staff at any of the hyperscalers, GTM wizards who scaled something huge before. The point being, if what you’ve done in the past is a clear indicator of how fast and far you can go next, your trajectory makes you legible. Trusted relationships. A founder is legible when an investor believes they’re capable of huge things. Sometimes that belief is borne out of the investor’s firsthand knowledge. More often, it’s based on a referral from a trusted source. As a founder, the more of those “trusted sources” you can impress and cultivate, the more legible you become to a greater universe of investors. And while it’s hard to reach the highest echelon of trusted sources, relationships are a predictable path from outside to insider. Traction. The most democratic of all. As I like to say at Founder Day : Some founders raise on faith, but eventually, all founders raise on evidence. And if you get the evidence faster, I believe capital will follow. The bad news is that these days, the bar for traction and the size of its accompanying TAM are crushingly high. (And speaking of bias, some founders face an even higher believability bar.) The good news is that, in the process of achieving this ridiculously impressive traction, you’re also building a ridiculously promising business. None of the above is easy. If it was, anyone could do it. The fact that social media makes it look easy is false advertising, pure and simple. In the past, a great pitch deck was a ticket you needed to ride the VC train; these days, it’s more of a relic of days gone by. You still need an AI-parsable instrument of communication that quickly flags VCs the top reasons you’re worth meeting (at my firm we definitely want to see a deck or a memo ). You still need a compelling (and hopefully substantive) story that wins investors over. And you still need a great data room that codifies and simplifies every item of due diligence. But none of this needs to look like a pitch deck. Especially generic AI-generated slop. And hey, by the way? There’s always the other choice. If legibility feels out of reach, and you don’t want to FOMO and lie your way to a pre-seed, there is always that least-popular path: Don’t raise VC at all. Bootstrap your company, and get yourself to the best possible source of capital: revenue from loyal and happy customers. VC has done way too good a job convincing founders that ours is the best and only way. When in reality, it’s not for everyone and it’s bad for most. Besides, it’s crazy how much you can accomplish with AI these days. Haven’t you heard? 😉 The early-rate deadline for the World Changing Ideas Awards is Friday, November 13, at 11:59 p.m. PT. Apply today .

articles.title: Legacy Programming Critique Exposes Inherent Computational Limits of Modern Natural Language
articles.content: On the foolishness of "natural language programming". Since the early days of automatic computing we have had people that have felt it as a shortcoming that programming required the care and accuracy that is characteristic for the use of any formal symbolism. They blamed the mechanical slave for its strict obedience with which it carried out its given instructions, even if a moment's thought would have revealed that those instructions contained an obvious mistake. "But a moment is a long time, and thought is a painful process." (A.E.Housman). They eagerly hoped and waited for more sensible machinery that would refuse to embark on such nonsensical activities as a trivial clerical error evoked at the time. Machine code, with its absence of almost any form of redundancy, was soon identified as a needlessly risky interface between man and machine. Partly in response to this recognition so-called "high-level programming languages" were developed, and, as time went by, we learned to a certain extent how to enhance the protection against silly mistakes. It was a significant improvement that now many a silly mistake did result in an error message instead of in an erroneous answer. (And even this improvement wasn't universally appreciated: some people found error messages they couldn't ignore more annoying than wrong results, and, when judging the relative merits of programming languages, some still seem to equate "the ease of programming" with the ease of making undetected mistakes.) The (abstract) machine corresponding to a programming language remained, however, a faithful slave, i.e. the nonsensible automaton perfectly capable of carrying out nonsensical instructions. Programming remained the use of a formal symbolism and, as such, continued to require the care and accuracy required before. In order to make machines significantly easier to use, it has been proposed (to try) to design machines that we could instruct in our native tongues. this would, admittedly, make the machines much more complicated, but, it was argued, by letting the machine carry a larger share of the burden, life would become easier for us. It sounds sensible provided you blame the obligation to use a formal symbolism as the source of your difficulties. But is the argument valid? I doubt. We know in the meantime that the choice of an interface is not just a division of (a fixed amount of) labour, because the work involved in co-operating and communicating across the interface has to be added. We know in the meantime —from sobering experience, I may add— that a change of interface can easily increase at both sides of the fence the amount of work to be done (even drastically so). Hence the increased preference for what are now called "narrow interfaces". Therefore, although changing to communication between machine and man conducted in the latter's native tongue would greatly increase the machine's burden, we have to challenge the assumption that this would simplify man's life. A short look at the history of mathematics shows how justified this challenge is. Greek mathematics got stuck because it remained a verbal, pictorial activity, Moslem "algebra", after a timid attempt at symbolism, died when it returned to the rhetoric style, and the modern civilized world could only emerge —for better or for worse— when Western Europe could free itself from the fetters of medieval scholasticism —a vain attempt at verbal precision!— thanks to the carefully, or at least consciously designed formal symbolisms that we owe to people like Vieta, Descartes, Leibniz, and (later) Boole. The virtue of formal texts is that their manipulations, in order to be legitimate, need to satisfy only a few simple rules; they are, when you come to think of it, an amazingly effective tool for ruling out all sorts of nonsense that, when we use our native tongues, are almost impossible to avoid. Instead of regarding the obligation to use formal symbols as a burden, we should regard the convenience of using them as a privilege: thanks to them, school children can learn to do what in earlier days only genius could achieve. (This was evidently not understood by the author that wrote —in 1977— in the preface of a technical report that "even the standard symbols used for logical connectives have been avoided for the sake of clarity". The occurrence of that sentence suggests that the author's misunderstanding is not confined to him alone.) When all is said and told, the "naturalness" with which we use our native tongues boils down to the ease with which we can use them for making statements the nonsense of which is not obvious. It may be illuminating to try to imagine what would have happened if, right from the start our native tongue would have been the only vehicle for the input into and the output from our information processing equipment. My considered guess is that history would, in a sense, have repeated itself, and that computer science would consist mainly of the indeed black art how to bootstrap from there to a sufficiently well-defined formal system. We would need all the intellect in the world to get the interface narrow enough to be usable, and, in view of the history of mankind, it may not be overly pessimistic to guess that to do the job well enough would require again a few thousand years. Remark. As a result of the educational trend away from intellectual discipline, the last decades have shown in the Western world a sharp decline of people's mastery of their own language: many people that by the standards of a previous generation should know better, are no longer able to use their native tongue effectively, even for purposes for which it is pretty adequate.
